final.title: Tool consolidation is a design constraint, not a rebuild
final.body:
If you run a 1–10 person business, tool consolidation is not mainly a software question. It is a design choice: keep the stack you already use, and add one thin automation layer only where the handoff is repeated, rule-based, and worth the extra moving part. Replacing every app usually creates more switching cost than it removes.

A practical test is simple. List the tools involved in one recurring workflow, then trace the manual handoffs between them: CRM, email, invoicing, documents, calendar, and so on. Mark the step that causes the most delay or error. If that handoff repeats every week, touches two or more tools, and has a clear outcome, it may be a good candidate for a bounded workflow. That example is a selection rule, not a claim about what every business should automate.

For Bareni, the boundary stays plain. We work inside your own accounts, and the accounts, automation tools, and API access stay in the customer's name from the start. That is policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty. Human approval stays mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions. Bareni also currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work, bulk cold-email automation, and scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows as scope discipline.

So the next step is to map one recurring handoff and ask: does consolidation reduce friction, or just rearrange it? If it only rearranges it, leave the stack alone.
